# EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies

Stuart Farmer Affiliation: Casa Dilauro Independent Research
([casadilauro.com](https://casadilauro.com))
Email: [](mailto:)[stuart@casadilauro.com](mailto:stuart@casadilauro.com)
Affiliation: [github.com/StuartFarmer/elitetable](https://github.com/StuartFarmer/elitetable)

 

EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search  
for Executable Control Policies

 

Stuart Farmer  
Casa Dilauro Independent Research
([casadilauro.com](https://casadilauro.com))

[stuart@casadilauro.com](mailto:stuart@casadilauro.com)

[github.com/StuartFarmer/elitetable](https://github.com/StuartFarmer/elitetable)

 

Abstract—EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided
by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of
high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing
solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated
across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty
candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten
independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between
the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner
search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner
reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten
searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six
tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their
reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out
episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results
document improvement during program search and the transfer of
selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and
ablations are needed to establish EliteTable’s relative performance and
the contributions of its components.

 

## 1  Introduction

This work was motivated by the broader study of recursive
self-improvement and LLM-guided program search: how these algorithms are
structured, which tasks they address, how well their solutions
generalize, and which mechanisms support improvement.

The study examines one part of that motivation: whether a program-search
algorithm inspired by prior work can also show improvement through
repeated evaluation and revision.

In program search, one part of the improvement loop proposes a solution,
often source code or an executable policy. Another part, the evaluator,
provides a score or feedback on how that solution performs on the task.

Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) illustrates this feedback pattern: a
language model receives a task description and previously evaluated
solutions, then uses that feedback to propose further
solutions \[[1](#bib.bib1)\].

FunSearch makes this feedback loop concrete for executable programs. It
uses an island-based database of solutions, maintaining multiple
populations to support diversity. Its applications include cap-set
constructions and online bin-packing heuristics \[[2](#bib.bib2)\].

AlphaEvolve extends evolutionary code modification to scientific and
computational problems, using evaluator feedback to guide
revisions \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]. In these systems, evaluation gives program
search an external measure of whether a proposed change is useful.

These algorithms differ in what they retain and how they generate
candidates. ShinkaEvolve combines parent sampling, code-novelty
rejection, and bandit-based selection among language
models \[[4](#bib.bib4)\].

Evolution of Heuristics evolves descriptions of heuristic ideas together
with their executable implementations, giving the language model both
conceptual and code-level information about the solutions it
explores \[[5](#bib.bib5)\].

EliteTable draws on these approaches through a fixed-capacity table of
high-scoring programs. New candidates compete with retained solutions
after each generation, while three operators generate fresh proposals,
edits, and remixes. The design aims to provide a simple feedback loop
for repeated program improvement.

Keeping incumbents eligible guarantees that the best recorded search
score cannot decrease, but does not guarantee that newly generated
solutions improve. A search may retain elites based on similar
heuristics and become confined to a local optimum \[[2](#bib.bib2)\].
Selected solutions may also fail to generalize to new episodes, so
held-out evaluation is necessary \[[10](#bib.bib10)\].

The study asks two questions. First, do in-sample winner scores and
candidate-score distributions improve across generations? Second, do
selected-winner gains transfer to held-out episodes? I examine these
questions across six Gymnasium control tasks \[[7](#bib.bib7)\].

Records were kept for every candidate across the sixty searches. Between
generations one and ten, pooled candidate-score medians increased in all
six tasks and median selected-winner search scores increased in five.
CartPole-v1 winners were already at the ceiling in generation one.

In CarRacing-v3, the candidate population showed a bimodal score
distribution: a higher-return concentration moved toward stronger scores
across generations while a low-return group persisted.

Held-out evaluation addressed the second question. All ten paired
endpoint changes were positive in four tasks. Acrobot-v1’s median paired
held-out change was negative. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved
between the first and final evaluations, but neither reached its
reporting target.

Held-out gains were not necessarily monotonic: intermediate performance
sometimes declined. Longer searches might produce further gains, but the
tested budget does not establish whether BipedalWalker-v3 or
CarRacing-v3 would eventually reach their targets.

### 2.1  Generation and repair

EliteTable uses three operators: new, edit, and remix. Generation one
contains only fresh proposals; the top $`K`$ evaluated solutions enter
the elite table. Subsequent generations use the allocation in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Study structure ‣ 3 Experimental Design ‣ EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Searchfor Executable Control Policies").
Fresh proposals receive elite descriptions and scores, edits receive one
parent’s source, and remixes combine information from up to three
parents. Parents are sampled uniformly from the table frozen at the
start of the generation.

Before evaluation, proposed solutions are checked for schema compliance,
valid source edits, and parseable Python syntax using the abstract
syntax tree (AST).

Solutions must satisfy the required policy interface and pass duplicate
checks. Duplicate detection compares AST structures rather than source
text.

Solutions are then passed to the evaluator. Validation or execution
failures, such as access to an undefined variable, return diagnostics to
a repair loop so the model can revise the proposal.

If the revised solution still fails, it returns to the repair loop, up
to five repairs per candidate slot.

Candidate timeouts are treated as failures, not zero-reward episodes or
successful truncations. Infrastructure failures interrupt execution
rather than enter the candidate-repair loop.

1: Task, fixed LLM, search panel; $`T=10`$, $`N=50`$, $`K=10`$

2: $`\mathcal{E}_{0}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

3: for $`t=1,\ldots,T`$ do

4:   Freeze parent table at $`\mathcal{E}_{t-1}`$

5:   Allocate new/edit/remix slots
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Study structure ‣ 3 Experimental Design ‣ EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Searchfor Executable Control Policies"))

6:   Apply empty/single-elite fallbacks; shuffle slots

7:   Sample parents uniformly; remix parents are distinct

8:   $`\mathcal{C}_{t}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

9:   for all candidate slots do

10:    Generate program; validate, evaluate, and repair

11:    Add successful evaluated program to $`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$

12:   end for

13:   Wait for every slot to finish or be discarded

14:
  $`\mathcal{E}_{t}\leftarrow\operatorname{TopK}(\mathcal{E}_{t-1}\cup\mathcal{C}_{t})`$

15:   Archive the search-selected winner in $`\mathcal{E}_{t}`$

16: end for

17: Evaluate archived winners on held-out episodes

Algorithm 1 EliteTable search

### 2.2  Elite selection

As briefly mentioned, EliteTable retains the highest-scoring programs
across completed generations. For elite capacity $`K`$, the update rule
is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{E}_{t}=\operatorname{TopK}\left(\mathcal{E}_{t-1}\cup\mathcal{C}_{t}\right).
``` |  | (1) |

Here $`\mathcal{E}_{t}`$ is the retained elite set after generation
$`t`$, $`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$ contains valid new candidates from that
generation, and $`\operatorname{TopK}`$ selects up to $`K`$ programs.
Candidates are ranked by descending mean search reward.

For equal scores, edits take priority over remixes, followed by
incumbent elites and then fresh proposals. Any remaining ties are
resolved by ascending organism identifier.

This persistent elitist mechanism ensures that the highest recorded
*search-panel* reward cannot decrease between completed generations,
assuming previously recorded evaluations remain unchanged. This
monotonicity does not imply monotonic held-out performance.

## 3  Experimental Design

### 3.1  Study structure

Six control environments were selected from the Gymnasium reinforcement
learning library \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. Their task profiles are listed in
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 EliteTable Program Search ‣ EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Searchfor Executable Control Policies").

The tasks were selected for their perceived differences in difficulty
and their variety of observation and action spaces.

Across the sixty searches, hyperparameters were chosen to balance
computational cost against the opportunity for improvement.

|  Hyperparameter               |  Setting                       |
|-------------------------------|--------------------------------|
|  Tasks                        |  6                             |
|  Searches per task            |  10                            |
|  Population size              |  50                            |
|  Elite table size             |  10                            |
|  Generations                  |  10                            |
|  Initial operator split       |  100% new, 0% edit, 0% remix   |
|  Subsequent operator split    |  20% new, 40% edit, 40% remix  |
|  Search initialization seeds  |  $`\{0,\ldots,9\}`$            |
|  In-sample seeds              |  $`\{0,\ldots,9\}`$            |
|  Out-of-sample seeds          |  $`\{1000,\ldots,1099\}`$      |
|  Maximum repairs per slot     |  5                             |
|  Early stopping?              |  False                         |

The subsequent operator split applies when at least two elites are
available. Held-out episodes are evaluated per distinct generation
winner within each search.

Table 2: Shared search and evaluation settings.

Each candidate slot includes its initial proposal and any repair
attempts; it either produces an evaluated policy or is discarded. Slot
counts therefore differ from counts of valid programs, model requests,
and completed episode evaluations.

The study records the configuration and execution history of each
search. Initialization seeds control operator scheduling and parent
sampling, but do not make hosted model responses deterministic.
Reproduction can therefore follow the recorded procedure without
guaranteeing identical search trajectories.

### 3.2  Environments and policy interface

Generated solutions must implement Solution(Policy), a Python class with
an asynchronous action method. Policy objects receive the current
observation, observation and action spaces, and task instructions.

The policy interacts with the environment through an observe–act loop.
Its runtime interface does not expose reward values or environment
internals.

A policy may retain state within an episode, provided it satisfies the
required interface. That state must be reset at the start of each
episode.

Generation and repair prompts include task documentation, resolved
environment settings, the observation/action contract, the objective,
and execution constraints. This documented task knowledge is distinct
from the information exposed to a policy during execution.

For BipedalWalker-v3, the prompts also include explicit observation
indexing, normalization, motor ordering, and reward details. Prompt
construction is configurable by task.

The study therefore evaluates program search with documented task
knowledge, rather than learning solely from interaction.

### 3.3  Model configuration

I used the requested model route openai/gpt-oss-120b:nitro through
OpenRouter for proposal generation and repair.

Responses were capped at 16,384 tokens per request.

The runner does not explicitly set temperature or top-$`p`$, so the
study does not specify fixed values for those parameters. Returned
model, provider, and usage metadata are retained when available. The
requested route does not guarantee identical provider execution across
requests.

Because fresh proposals receive elite summaries, they cannot serve as a
history-independent sampling baseline.

### 3.4  Fitness and held-out evaluation

For policy $`\pi`$, its episode return under seed $`s`$ is the
undiscounted sum

|     |                                     |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(\pi,s)=\sum_{t=0}^{T_{s}-1}r_{t},
       ```                                  |     | (2) |

where $`T_{s}`$ is the number of steps before environment termination or
the configured step cap.

Candidate fitness is the arithmetic mean over the ten fixed search seeds
$`S=\{0,\ldots,9\}`$:

|     |                                           |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       F(\pi)=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{s\in S}R(\pi,s).
       ```                                        |     | (3) |

EliteTable ranks candidates by higher fitness scores. Tasks formulated
as minimization problems would require an appropriate score
transformation.

All candidate slots must finish evaluation or be discarded before the
elite table is updated. The top $`K`$ programs are then selected from
the new evaluated candidates and existing elites, using the tie-breaking
order described above.

After search finishes, the fixed historical winner from every generation
is evaluated on 100 held-out episode seeds,

|     |                         |     |
|-----|-------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       H=\{1000,\ldots,1099\},
       ```                      |     |

which are disjoint from both the search panel and the previously
inspected pilot panel 100–199.

Each distinct selected policy is evaluated once per held-out seed within
a search. Repeated generation winners within that search reuse cached
measurements. Held-out outcomes do not influence generation, repair,
promotion, stopping, or winner selection.

For environment $`e`$, search $`i`$, and generation $`g`$, held-out
performance is

|     |                                                           |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       Y_{e,i,g}=\frac{1}{100}\sum_{s\in H}R(\pi^{*}_{e,i,g},s),
       ```                                                        |     | (4) |

where $`\pi^{*}_{e,i,g}`$ is the winner selected by search fitness.

A valid held-out mean requires finite returns on all 100 specified seeds
and no recorded evaluation failures. Partial means are excluded. Missing
evaluations remain missing; they are not replaced with zero or rerun.

The paired held-out change is $`\Delta_{e,i}=Y_{e,i,10}-Y_{e,i,1}`$. I
report the median of these ten within-search changes for each task,
rather than the difference between the first- and final-generation
medians.

Descriptive 95% percentile intervals use 10,000 bootstrap resamples of
the ten whole-search paired records, with replacement. Each resample
preserves the within-search pairing and recomputes the median change.
These intervals describe variation conditional on the fixed episode
panels and tested configuration; they do not establish robustness across
new panels or models.

As a retrospective exploratory analysis, I applied two-sided exact
paired sign tests \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] to the ten endpoint changes per
task. The null is $`\Pr(\Delta>0\mid\Delta\neq 0)=1/2`$, not equality of
mean returns. Exact zero changes are excluded from sign counts. Holm
adjustment \[[12](#bib.bib12)\] covers all six tasks, retaining an
all-tied task as $`p=1`$ for correction only. These tests assume
independent searches and condition on the fixed episode panels and
tested configuration. They do not establish comparative superiority or
causal operator effects.

Figure 2: Candidate search-return distributions across generations,
pooled over ten searches per task. Solid blue lines show pooled
candidate medians; faint lines show medians within individual searches.
Violin widths show smoothed density, not operator membership or
independent replication.

### 3.5  Execution and reproducibility

Sixty searches were completed: ten initialization seeds across six
tasks. Each began at generation zero with no existing solutions.
Evaluation ran on an AMD64 host using eight worker processes, with up to
25 concurrent model operations for generation and repair. The configured
deadlines were 45 seconds per episode, ten seconds per policy action,
and 120 seconds per model-operation attempt.

The episode and action deadlines exclude Docker startup, queueing, and
final cleanup. Generated policies ran in Docker containers with
networking disabled, a read-only root filesystem, and resource limits.

Core reproduction code and recorded evidence are available at
[https://github.com/StuartFarmer/elitetable](https://github.com/StuartFarmer/elitetable).
The accompanying reproduction guide identifies the pinned revision and
offline reconstruction commands. The retrospective sign-test extension
and additional inputs and scripts for supplemental analyses accompany
this manuscript locally; they are not included in that pinned public
release. Reconstructing recorded results and running new stochastic
searches are distinct procedures.

## 4  Experimental Results

### 4.1  Completion and improvement during search

All sixty searches completed. Held-out measurements were available for
599 of 600 generation-winner panels. The missing MountainCar-v0
search-seed-8 panel was at generation six and did not affect any
endpoint pair.

Median selected-winner search scores increased between the first and
final generations in five environments. CartPole-v1 winners were already
at the score ceiling in generation one.

Newly evaluated candidate medians rose between generations one and ten
in all six tasks, including CartPole-v1.
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 Fitness and held-out evaluation ‣ 3 Experimental Design ‣ EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Searchfor Executable Control Policies")
shows these population changes, extending the evidence beyond retention
of strong initial winners.

These distributions contain newly evaluated candidates, not retained
elites or held-out winners. Each score averages ten search episodes;
failed or discarded candidates without scores are excluded. The
LunarLander-v3 display is restricted to returns between $`-1000`$ and
$`350`$: 198 scores outside this range remain in the calculations.

Candidate-score distributions show bimodality in some tasks. This
motivated an exploratory analysis of whether fresh proposals, edits, and
remixes contribute differently to the score mixture. The operator
analyses appear in Supplemental Analyses.

### 4.2  Performance on held-out episodes

Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.5 Execution and reproducibility ‣ 3 Experimental Design ‣ EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Searchfor Executable Control Policies")
reports paired endpoints and target counts. All ten searches improved in
each of four environments: MountainCar-v0, LunarLander-v3,
BipedalWalker-v3, and CarRacing-v3. CartPole-v1 remained at the ceiling,
while six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined. BipedalWalker-v3 and
CarRacing-v3 improved without a final winner reaching the reporting
target.

Each of the four tasks with ten positive changes has raw $`p=0.00195`$
and Holm-adjusted $`p=0.01172`$. For Acrobot-v1, raw $`p=0.75391`$ and
adjusted $`p=1`$, so the observed negative median does not establish a
systematic decline. The ten CartPole-v1 ties provide no informative sign
test and do not establish equivalence.

Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.5 Execution and reproducibility ‣ 3 Experimental Design ‣ EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Searchfor Executable Control Policies")
shows how outcomes develop across generations. Held-out scores sometimes
decline even when the endpoint improves. Acrobot-v1’s positive search
gains coexist with a negative median paired held-out change, consistent
with possible selection-panel specialization. The study shows transfer
of endpoint gains to new episodes in four tasks, but does not establish
robustness across task families or rule out overfitting. Broader
evaluation and comparisons with other search and reinforcement-learning
methods are needed.

### 4.3  Candidate reliability and resource use

Of 30,000 candidate slots, 29,959 reached evaluated status (99.9%) and
41 were discarded. The logs contain 38,289 model calls, including 8,287
repair calls, or 21.6% of all calls. Repair calls amount to 27.6% of the
30,000 initial proposal calls; because a slot may undergo multiple
repairs, this is not the percentage of proposals needing repair. The
completion rate describes the combined procedure and does not isolate
the repair loop’s contribution.

## 5  Discussion and Conclusion

The rising candidate-score medians show progress beyond retaining a
single strong initial solution. Newly generated populations also shift
toward higher returns. In four tasks, every final selected winner
improved over its first-generation counterpart on the fixed held-out
episode panel. These endpoint gains do not by themselves rule out
overfitting to the selection panel.

Acrobot-v1 exposes a limitation: search scores rose while the median
paired held-out change was negative. Further examination is needed to
identify the cause. Held-out evaluation covers each generation’s
selected winner, not every retained elite, so it does not describe the
full elite population. Search used ten episode seeds, compared with 100
held-out seeds. Future studies could test whether broader selection
panels reduce specialization; the current design does not isolate that
effect.

BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their
reporting targets. The tested budget does not establish whether
additional generations would eventually solve these tasks. Their gains
should therefore be distinguished from task attainment.

### 5.1  Program search and neural-policy training

EliteTable revises policy source code rather than updating neural-policy
weights through policy gradients. Source edits can change numerical
constants as well as program structure. Policy-gradient methods instead
update parameterized policies, often neural networks, using estimates of
the gradient of expected return with respect to policy
parameters \[[8](#bib.bib8)\].

The selected tasks are drawn from Gymnasium’s standard
reinforcement-learning environments \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. Matched
comparisons are needed to assess the relative strengths of program
search and neural-policy training on these tasks.

Source revisions can alter control structures, numerical constants,
state, and execution flow. Programmatic reinforcement learning can also
combine program search with guidance from a trained neural
policy \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. These are different update mechanisms; the
present study provides no matched comparison of their learning
efficiency.

### 5.2  Limitations and next steps

Understanding EliteTable’s components requires ablations and comparisons
with other systems. The observed improvements cannot yet be attributed
specifically to reuse, editing, remixing, retention, or repair. Ten
searches per environment quantify variation under fixed episode panels,
but do not establish robustness across episode distributions, language
models, prompts, or search configurations. The tasks are well known, so
the model may have encountered descriptions or potential solutions
during training.

Time-based deadlines can produce different outcomes on different
hardware. Hosted-provider variation can also change model outputs and
search trajectories, even when the same model route is requested.

The final solutions are Python programs available for inspection, but
source availability alone does not establish human interpretability.

I would prioritize budget-matched comparisons with other program-search
algorithms, including a history-independent generation baseline,
followed by complete-search ablations and comparisons across language
models. Longer budgets, new episode panels, and other task families
would test the limits of the observations. The present results provide
development evidence for those designs rather than confirmatory evidence
of comparative superiority.

### 5.3  Conclusion

EliteTable contributes to the study of self-improving LLM-assisted
program search. Across sixty searches, candidate populations improved on
selection episodes, while held-out evaluation distinguished transferable
gains, saturation, and regression. This work supports further
investigation of repeated program improvement as part of the broader
agenda toward recursive self-improvement. It does not test a system that
modifies its own optimizer or language model.

## Supplemental Analyses

 

All analyses use the same sixty completed searches. Core reproduction
code is available in the public GitHub repository. Prompts, policy
sources, and additional analysis inputs accompany this manuscript
locally; the reproduction guide identifies additions outside the pinned
public release.

## S1  Candidate populations during search

### S1.1  Population and winner endpoints

I first compared candidate and selected-winner scores in the first and
final generations to distinguish progress in newly generated programs
from retention of strong incumbents. For each task, I pooled evaluated
candidates across ten searches and calculated their median search score.
Separately, I calculated the median score of the ten selected generation
winners. Scores average returns on ten fixed search episodes; discarded
candidates without scores are excluded.

|                  | Candidates |         | Winners |         |
|------------------|------------|---------|---------|---------|
| Environment      | Gen. 1     | Gen. 10 | Gen. 1  | Gen. 10 |
| CartPole-v1      | 21.00      | 500.00  | 500.00  | 500.00  |
| MountainCar-v0   | -200.00    | -120.25 | -120.30 | -114.90 |
| Acrobot-v1       | -500.00    | -82.70  | -82.00  | -74.55  |
| LunarLander-v3   | -423.92    | 125.80  | -32.79  | 258.04  |
| BipedalWalker-v3 | -106.43    | -30.77  | -39.60  | -7.58   |
| CarRacing-v3     | -60.03     | 555.07  | 226.05  | 775.30  |

Table S1: Candidate and selected-winner medians at generations one and
ten.

New-candidate medians increased in all six environments. Selected-winner
medians increased in five, as CartPole-v1 winners were already at the
ceiling. These results show progress in the programs being generated
beyond retention of a strong early winner.

Generation one contains only fresh proposals, whereas later generations
mix fresh proposals, edits, and remixes. The population changes include
this composition change. This analysis does not isolate an operator
effect or establish held-out improvement of the full candidate
population.

### S1.2  CarRacing-v3 distribution across generations

I also examined the full CarRacing-v3 candidate-score distribution to
determine whether rising medians reflected a broad shift or the
disappearance of weak candidates. For each generation, I pooled
evaluated scores across ten searches and estimated a Gaussian kernel
density with a common bandwidth of 25 return units. Multiplying each
density by its evaluated-candidate count gives a band whose area equals
that count.

The ten generations are stacked from bottom to top. A colored band’s
*thickness* gives that generation’s count density; its cumulative upper
boundary is not the density. All 4,992 evaluated scores are included,
with 498–500 candidates per generation. Eight discarded slots have no
score. Scores average ten selection episodes, and smoothing extends
beyond the observed score range.

Figure S1: CarRacing-v3 candidate distributions over ten generations.

Higher-return concentrations emerge and move toward stronger scores as
generations advance. Weak candidates persist, but the distribution
shifts toward higher returns. These are in-sample changes under a
changing operator mixture, not evidence of population-wide held-out
gains.

## S2  Held-out outcomes and sensitivity

### S2.1  Paired search endpoints

I evaluated each search’s first and final selected winner on the same
100 held-out episodes. Winners were selected exclusively by search
scores; held-out returns did not affect selection. Pairing within each
search makes improvement and regression visible without pooling reward
scales across tasks.

Hollow circles mark the first generation and filled points mark the
final generation. Rightward movement indicates improvement; dashed lines
mark reporting targets. Panel headings give the numbers of improved
searches and final target-reaching winners. Each task retains its own
reward scale.

Figure S2: First and final held-out performance for all sixty searches.

All ten endpoint pairs improved in MountainCar-v0, LunarLander-v3,
BipedalWalker-v3, and CarRacing-v3. CartPole-v1 remained at the ceiling,
while six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined. BipedalWalker-v3 and
CarRacing-v3 improved without a final winner reaching the reporting
target.

All sixty endpoint pairs are available. The missing MountainCar-v0
search-seed-8 panel at generation six affects only the intermediate
trajectory.

### S2.2  Sensitivity to individual searches

For each task, I computed the ten paired held-out changes from
generation one to generation ten. I omitted one search at a time and
recomputed the median of the remaining nine changes. The minimum and
maximum of these ten medians measure sensitivity to an individual
search; they are not confidence intervals.

CP, MC and AC denote CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0 and Acrobot-v1; LL, BW
and CR denote LunarLander-v3, BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3. The
final rows give the full-sample median and leave-one-search-out (LOO)
range.

Table S2: Paired held-out changes and leave-one-search-out medians.

Omitting any one search leaves the direction of every task’s median
change unchanged. This check concerns variation among the ten searches
under common episode panels. It does not establish robustness to new
episode panels, prompts, or models.

Endpoint gains also need not be monotonic. At least one
adjacent-generation decline occurred in one CartPole-v1, five
MountainCar-v0, ten Acrobot-v1, ten LunarLander-v3, seven
BipedalWalker-v3 and nine CarRacing-v3 searches. LunarLander-v3’s median
fell from 179.38 at generation six to 168.29 at generation seven before
reaching 214.04. CarRacing-v3 fell from 683.81 at generation seven to
658.00 at generation eight before reaching 691.81.

## S3  Resource accounting

I aggregated model-call logs, candidate repair counters, discarded
slots, and recorded attempt durations across ten searches per task. All
sixty searches began at generation zero and finished in one recorded
attempt; none resumed a previous search.

For reward-scale context, I also evaluated a random-action policy on the
100-episode held-out panel and report the median of its run-level mean
returns. This is not a budget-matched program-search baseline. Calls,
repairs, discarded slots (Disc.), and hours are summed across searches.
Hours include reporting as well as search.

| Task             | Random  | Calls | Repairs | Disc. | Hours |
|------------------|---------|-------|---------|-------|-------|
| CartPole-v1      | 21.87   | 7134  | 2134    | 17    | 4.56  |
| MountainCar-v0   | -200.00 | 6157  | 1157    | 0     | 6.05  |
| Acrobot-v1       | -500.00 | 6546  | 1546    | 9     | 4.60  |
| LunarLander-v3   | -200.81 | 6269  | 1269    | 3     | 4.05  |
| BipedalWalker-v3 | -101.02 | 6064  | 1064    | 4     | 7.87  |
| CarRacing-v3     | -32.68  | 6119  | 1117    | 8     | 29.76 |
| Total            | —       | 38289 | 8287    | 41    | 56.88 |

Table S3: Random-action returns and recorded resources by task.

The logs contain 38,289 model calls, including 8,287 repair calls.
Repairs account for approximately 21.6% of logged calls, so
candidate-slot counts understate model usage. Of 30,000 slots, 29,959
(99.9%) reached evaluated status and 41 were discarded.

Recorded attempt durations total 56.88 hours, including 29.76 hours for
CarRacing-v3. These are neither CPU-hours nor elapsed wall time for the
whole study. Two logged calls lack usage records, so complete token and
monetary totals remain unknown.

## S4  Operator distributions and elite admission

### S4.1  CarRacing-v3 candidate distributions

I grouped CarRacing-v3 candidates by generation operator to examine how
fresh proposals, edits, and remixes contributed to the score mixture.
Generations two, six, and ten represent early, middle, and final
post-initialization search, pooling ten searches at each generation.

For each operator and generation, I estimated a Gaussian kernel density
with bandwidth 25 return units and multiplied it by the
evaluated-candidate count. Band thickness gives count density; band area
gives that operator’s candidate count. Shared axes and bandwidth support
comparison. Counts appear above each panel; the discarded slot at
generation six is excluded. Smoothing extends beyond observed returns.

Figure S3: CarRacing-v3 score distributions by generation operator.

All three operators contribute to the early low-score concentration. By
generation ten, fresh proposals remain concentrated at low scores while
edits and remixes supply most of the higher-score population. Unequal
allocation, parent selection, and inherited information prevent
attributing these differences solely to operator choice.

### S4.2  Admission to the elite table

I extended the analysis by measuring how often an evaluated candidate
entered the elite table in its birth generation, pooling generations
2–10 across ten searches per task. I grouped admissions by the operator
used to generate the candidate. Dividing admissions by each operator’s
evaluated-candidate count accounts for unequal allocations. This
measures entry into the table, not the duration of later retention.

Points give admission percentages, with admitted and evaluated counts
noted alongside. Discarded slots are excluded from the rate
denominators.

Figure S4: Birth-generation elite-admission rates by task and operator.

Only 55 of 5,394 evaluated fresh proposals entered the elite table,
approximately 1%. Fresh proposals had lower observed admission rates
under the tested configuration. They receive elite summaries but no
parent source, so they are not a history-independent sampling baseline.

Incumbent competition and deterministic tie-breaking also affect
admission. CartPole-v1’s equal-score priority for edits is especially
visible. The rates do not identify causal operator effects, and
candidates are dependent observations within searches.
````
